opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we think about a lot. My general philosophy is to be pretty conservative about what you change. Over the last decade the field has converged on a small set of really robust building blocks: transformers, attention, layer norm, residual connections, the standard training recipes, the optimizers people actually use at scale. Those things have been battle-tested across language, images, video, audio. So when I move into a new modality, my default is to keep as much of that core machinery as possible and ask, "What's the minimum I actually need to change to make this work?"

Usually the place where you *do* have to innovate is at the boundaries: how you get data into the model and how you get it back out. What's the right representation? What's the right tokenization or latent space? How do you structure the problem so the model can actually learn the thing you care about? For something like 3D or spatial data, the representation question is huge, because there isn't one obvious canonical format the way there is with pixels or text. That's where I'd rather spend my innovation budget.

The reason is partly practical. Every time you introduce a novel architectural component, you take on risk. You don't know how it scales, you don't know its failure modes, and you lose the ability to lean on all the infrastructure, kernels, and tricks the community has built up. I've seen a lot of papers over the years with clever, bespoke architectures that look great at small scale and then just get steamrolled by a vanilla transformer with more data and compute. That's the bitter lesson playing out again and again.

So the heuristic is: keep the general-purpose stuff that's proven to scale, and be really deliberate about the handful of places where your modality genuinely has different structure. If you can't articulate why the standard approach fails for your problem, you probably shouldn't be replacing it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to keep proven architecture components when moving to a new modality and change only what is needed, so the modality alone does not justify discarding what already works.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so my bias here is pretty strong, and it comes from having lived through the transition from the CNN era to the transformer era. For a long time, every modality had its own bespoke architecture. If you worked on images, you had convnets with all this hand-designed structure baked in. If you worked on language, you had RNNs or LSTMs. If you did 3D, you had point cloud networks or voxel grids with their own inductive biases. And the lesson of the last several years is that almost all of that specialization got washed out. The transformer basically ate everything.

So when we started thinking about 3D at World Labs, the default answer to "which architecture do we keep" is: keep the transformer, keep the training recipe, keep the infrastructure, and be very skeptical of anything modality-specific. The reason is that the transformer is less an architecture and more a substrate. It's a general-purpose way of mixing information across a set of tokens, and all of the scaling knowledge, the optimizer tricks, the parallelism, the kernels, everything the whole field has invested in, transfers for free. If you throw that away because 3D "feels different," you're rebuilding a decade of engineering by yourself.

The thing I actually think hard about is not the backbone, it's the tokenization and the representation. That's where the modality really lives. For language it's obvious, you have discrete tokens. For images, the ViT patch thing turned out to be good enough. For 3D the question is genuinely open. Is your unit a point, a voxel, a Gaussian, a latent patch of some encoder? Is the thing you're predicting the geometry, or the appearance, or some learned latent that's agnostic to both? Those decisions determine what the model can even express, and they're much more consequential than whether you use attention or something else.

And then the honest answer about how we decide is that we try to keep the architecture boring and spend our novelty budget on the data and the representation. Every time I've been tempted to add some clever 3D-specific module, a geometric prior or some equivariance thing, the question I ask is: will this still help when I have a hundred times more data? Usually the answer is no, the prior becomes a constraint, the model would have learned that structure anyway and then some. Occasionally the answer is yes, usually when the structure is something really fundamental like a camera projection that we know to be exactly true, and then it's worth baking in. But the bar is high.

The other thing I'd say is that you shouldn't underrate how much you can inherit from adjacent modalities. Video is really close to 3D. A video model has already learned a huge amount about geometry, occlusion, lighting, how things look from different viewpoints, it just hasn't been forced to make that explicit. So rather than asking "what's the right architecture for 3D," a lot of our thinking is "how do we get the stuff that video and image models already know and give it a 3D-consistent output," which is a different and I think more productive question.

r001.rationale: The response says to keep the transformer and be skeptical of modality-specific changes, warning against throwing out established architecture just because 3D feels different.

astra-6.text:
I tend to start by asking how far we can get with the architectures we already have. When you move to a new modality, there’s a temptation to say, “This data is fundamentally different, so we need a fundamentally different model.” Sometimes that’s true, but I’d rather establish a strong baseline before making that assumption.

The useful distinction is between the parts that need to understand the structure of the input and the parts that do the computation. You might need to change how you represent the data, how you break it into tokens, or what you ask the model to predict, while keeping much of the architecture intact.

Then you look at where that approach breaks down. Is it missing some important structure? Is it too expensive? Those failures give you a reason to introduce something specific to the modality. So my default is to reuse what works, and let experiments tell us where we need a new idea.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to establish a strong baseline with existing architectures and make a new model only when experiments show a need, so a new modality alone does not justify discarding what works.

sol-6.1.text:
I usually start by trying to change as little as possible. If an architecture works well in one modality, that’s a useful starting point for another. You learn a lot by asking: how far can we get with the same basic machinery, just changing how we represent the inputs and outputs?

Then you look at where it struggles. Is there something about the structure of this modality that the architecture isn’t capturing? Is the representation making the task unnecessarily difficult? Those are reasons to introduce something new. But I’d rather make those changes in response to a concrete failure than assume up front that every new modality needs a completely different architecture.

r001.rationale: The response says an architecture that works in one modality is a useful starting point and that a new modality does not automatically call for a completely different architecture.
